As of 150 AM EST Thursday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A gradually deepening surface low will track from the 
Ohio Valley east over southern New England before heading off into 
the Canadian Maritimes today into tomorrow. Despite a favorable 
storm track for snow, a marginally cold airmass will be in place at 
the onset, especially at the surface due to a lack of Canadian high 
pressure to the north. Precipitation will enter southwestern areas 
this morning but very slowly make its way northeast during the day. 
By tonight, it should reach the Northeast Kingdom, but the heaviest 
rates will remain to the south. It will likely never reach the St. 
Lawrence Valley though. At the onset, surface temperatures will be 
in the 30s in most places, with low 40s in the warmest valleys. 
Steep lapse rates will exist with summit levels well below freezing, 
though a lack of a significantly dry layer will prevent significant 
wet-bulb cooling. 

Precipitation will begin as rain in the valleys and snow at the 
summits. An estimate of initial snow levels is around 1,500 ft. 
Light rates and daytime occurrence will prevent significant 
accumulations at the onset outside the mountains. A weak November 
sun angle will limit some of the warming effects though. Heading 
into tonight, heavier rates should enter southern areas, and 
darkness will end any solar radiation. The combination of lowering 
temperatures due to dynamical cooling and nighttime cooling will 
allow snow levels to drop a bit, and especially allow for more 
efficient accumulations at higher elevations with higher snow 
ratios. By Friday morning, snow levels should be around or below 
1,000 ft. While brief periods of snow are possible in the low 
valleys like the Champlain Valley and the Lower Connecticut Valley, 
temperatures will likely stay just above freezing and prevent 
accumulations other than maybe some slush on grassy-type surfaces. 

As the low tracks to the east heading through Friday, cyclonic 
northwest flow will develop and maintain periods of upslope snow 
showers in the higher terrain through Saturday. Boundary layer 
temperatures will reach their lowest values Saturday morning, with 
most areas likely seeing temperatures in the 20s. However, that time 
period will likely be dry and prevent any snow from occurring in the 
valleys. Warm Lake Champlain temperatures will probably further 
limit the already marginal accumulations in the immediate Champlain 
Valley, especially with northwest flow off the lake and downsloping 
along the eastern Adirondacks. 

Confidence has increased in a more southerly storm track and a less 
impactful event. Our deterministic most-likely scenario has snow 
amounts in the 2-5 inch range for the southern Adirondacks, central 
Greens and southern Greens around and above 2,000 ft. Areas between 
1,000-2,000 ft look to be in the 0-2 inch range, and below 1,000 ft 
looks to be a slushy coating at most. The main area of uncertainty 
that remains is the potential for a mesoband to reach southern 
Vermont. If it reaches, brief accumulations are possible down to the 
valley floors due to dynamical cooling and an additional couple 
inches would be possible across the higher terrain. However, this 
should not significantly change the impacts. 

At this point, the snowfall looks too light to cause power outages 
but far southern Vermont will have to be watched in case the 
mesoband comes in and stalls there for a couple hours.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Models continue to suggest we could see a few upslope 
snow showers along the western slopes of the Green and Adirondack 
Mountains Sunday night into Monday morning. This may yield some 
minor snow accumulation but otherwise not impactful. Increasing 
subsidence from a building deep layer ridge will bring an end to any 
shower activity by Monday afternoon. High pressure will remain 
entrenched across the region through the remainder of the week with 
the axis of the upper level ridge forcing a series of disturbances 
to push harmlessly to our north. Temperatures will warm throughout 
the week with high temperatures by Wednesday and Thursday climbing 
into the 50s, which will be slightly above normal for this time of 
the year.
